citation.title: Blame the Machine? Insights From an Experiment on Algorithm Aversion and Blame Avoidance in Computer-Aided Human Resource Management

reading.source_scope_note: Human delegation decisions in a vignette-based employee-forecast experiment. The study does not directly measure conscious blame-avoidance motives, experienced blame or intrinsic AI moral decisions. Cited prior primary studies were not independently read here.
access_limits: All extracted article text, four figures’ captions and reported descriptions, three result tables, limitations and references read. Plots were not independently digitized.
Appendices A–C are linked supplementary material outside this 14-page file and were not read; raw data and supplementary interaction tests were not obtained.

study.design: Randomized 2×2 promotion-versus-dismissal frame and pretest-versus-no-test experience
study.outcome: Binary choice to tie ten employee-performance forecasts to an algorithm, with lottery-voucher incentives
study.scope: Convenience sample of predominantly German young professionals and graduate students

summary: 66 of 288 respondents delegated to the algorithm. Delegation was lower after pretesting. The overall promotion/dismissal contrast and the pretest×decision-type interaction were not significant. Confidence in human and algorithmic forecasts was associated with delegation, but confidence was measured after the choice. The findings qualify a simple unpleasant-decision-to-blame-avoidance story.

findings.term: Pretesting errors can increase algorithm aversion
findings.definition: Experiencing an algorithm’s imperfect forecasts reduced subsequent delegation in the studied task even though reported average forecast error was comparable to, and slightly lower than, human error.
findings.novelty_rationale: An additional empirical condition for algorithm aversion, not a new label for error exposure or distrust.

evidence.quote: supporting the baseline hypothesis H2a but not H2b.
We use this post-hoc measure for explorative analyses.

findings.evidence_scope: Randomized pretest exposure in an employee-forecast vignette. Overall delegation was 23%; pretesting decreased delegation. Confidence predictors were post-task observational measures rather than randomized mechanisms.
findings.boundary: The treatment combined practice and observing forecast performance. It does not isolate prediction error as the sole mediator, prove that all training reduces adoption, or imply that withholding model limitations is an appropriate remedy. Odds ratios are not percentage-point changes or probability ratios.

findings.term: Unpleasant-task delegation did not independently establish blame shielding
findings.definition: The promotion-versus-dismissal manipulation did not significantly change overall delegation, so this experiment does not show an unconditional tendency to evade responsibility by assigning dismissals to algorithms.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds an evidential boundary to existing agency laundering rather than assume every delegated adverse decision is a new responsibility-evasion behaviour.

findings.evidence_scope: Human forecast-source choices, not ratings by affected workers or a direct manipulation/measure of concealment intent. Decision-type effects and the interaction were nonsignificant in the reported tests.
findings.boundary: A nonsignificant frame effect does not prove blame avoidance never occurs. Nor do exploratory confidence subgroups prove the mechanism: their confidence was measured after treatment and delegation. No real dismissals, accountability escape or misleading explanation was observed.

methodological_limits: Only 288 of 574 reached complete responses, creating potential completion-selection limits despite randomized initial assignments; covariate regressions use 267 cases.
The highly educated convenience sample is not a representative sample of professional HR managers or all German residents.
Lottery vouchers and imagined employee decisions do not reproduce actual hiring, dismissal or affected-worker sanctions.
The pretest effect is significant in one decision-type subgroup and not the other, but the interaction is not significant. Unequal subgroup significance does not establish moderation.
Post-choice confidence may reflect rationalization or the task experience as well as prior trust; adjustment for it does not identify the causal confidence pathway.
Text sometimes describes odds-ratio changes as likelihood changes; this review preserves odds/probability distinctions.
The randomized choice framing does not identify an unmeasured latent psychological motive by itself, despite stronger causal-mechanism language in the introduction.
Secondary baseline demographic null results do not prove those variables never influence delegation.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Jauernig’s monetary procedure choices suggest a role for discretionary scope; Maasland’s pretest effect shows a different task and mechanism candidate. Neither should become a universal one-cause account of algorithm aversion.

A warning/practice intervention can change checking, selection accuracy and willingness to use advice in different ways. Reduced delegation is not automatically improved verification or decision quality.
Joo measures third-party blame shares, while Maasland measures delegation choices. Choosing a tool, displacing blame and deliberately obscuring responsibility remain separate outcomes.

deferred.reason: Named background strategy with relevant primary leads, but the current unpleasant-task hypothesis and interaction were not supported and the motive was not directly measured. Record the boundary rather than add a positive new behaviour from the hypothesis.
Discussed as an avenue for cross-cultural replication, not established as a distinct behavioural mechanism in this experiment.

limitations: No new standalone concept added; two existing entries gain a read empirical source and explicit counterevidence.
The paper’s partial replication claims were read but the Dietvorst originals were not independently reviewed in this step.
